spring.a: Spring is a popular Java framework for building enterprise applications. Its main idea is IoC (Inversion of Control) and DI (Dependency Injection) — Spring creates and connects your objects for you, so your code stays loosely coupled and easy to test. Modules: Core, AOP, Data/JDBC, ORM, Web MVC, Security, Test.

Normally you create objects with new. With IoC, control is inverted — the Spring container creates, configures, and manages objects (beans). Simple example: Instead of cooking yourself (creating objects), you order at a restaurant (Spring) and the dish is delivered to you.

DI is how IoC is implemented: Spring gives (injects) the objects a class needs instead of the class creating them. @Service public class OrderService { private final PaymentService paymentService; public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) { // Spring injects it this.paymentService = paymentService; } }

spring.q: Types of Dependency Injection? Which is best?
spring.a:
1. Constructor injection – via constructor (recommended: fields can be final, mandatory dependencies are clear, easy to unit test, no nulls).
2. Setter injection – via setter method (for optional dependencies).
3. Field injection – @Autowired directly on the field (easy but not recommended – hard to test, hides dependencies).
Any object that is created and managed by the Spring IoC container. You create beans with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, or @Bean methods.

spring.q: What is the IoC container? BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?
spring.a: The container creates beans, injects dependencies, and manages their life cycle. BeanFactory ApplicationContext Basic container Advanced container (extends BeanFactory) Lazy loading (creates bean when asked) Eager loading of singletons at startup No events, i18n, AOP support built-in Supports events, internationalization, AOP, annotations Rarely used today Used in all Spring Boot apps

Scope Meaning singleton (default) One object per Spring container prototype New object every time it's requested request One per HTTP request (web) session One per HTTP session (web) application One per ServletContext websocket One per WebSocket session @Scope("prototype")

No, not automatically. Spring creates only one instance, but if it has changeable (mutable) fields, multiple threads can corrupt them. Keep singleton beans stateless (no mutable fields), or use thread-safe structures.

spring.q: What happens if you inject a prototype bean into a singleton?
spring.a: The prototype is injected only once when the singleton is created, so it behaves like a singleton. Fix: use ObjectProvider<T>, @Lookup method, or scoped proxy.

spring.q: Explain the Spring Bean life cycle.
spring.a:
1. Container starts → Bean instantiated (constructor).
2. Dependencies injected.
3. Aware interfaces called (BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware).
4. BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization().
5. Init method – @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet() / custom init.
6. BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization() (proxies for AOP created here).
7. Bean ready to use.
8. On shutdown → Destroy – @PreDestroy / destroy().

All create beans (all are specializations of @Component). The difference is meaning/layer: @Component – generic bean. @Service – business logic layer. @Repository – data access layer; also translates DB exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException. @Controller – web layer (returns views); @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody (returns JSON).

@Component @Bean On a class On a method inside @Configuration class Auto-detected by component scanning Declared manually For your own classes For third-party classes you can't annotate (e.g., RestTemplate, ObjectMapper) @Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean public RestTemplate restTemplate() { return new RestTemplate(); } }

spring.q: What is @Autowired? How does it resolve beans?
spring.a: Tells Spring to inject a dependency. It matches by type first. If there are multiple beans of the same type → uses @Qualifier or @Primary, then the field/parameter name. If none found → error (unless required = false).

When there are 2+ beans of the same type (e.g., UpiPayment and CardPayment both implement PaymentService): @Primary – marks the default bean to use. @Qualifier("cardPayment") – picks a specific bean at the injection point. Qualifier wins over Primary.
NoUnique – more than one bean matches and Spring can't choose (fix with @Qualifier/@Primary). NoSuch – no bean of that type exists (missing annotation, or class outside the component-scan package).
Tells Spring which packages to scan for @Component classes. In Spring Boot, @SpringBootApplication scans the package of the main class and its sub-packages automatically.
Marks a class that contains @Bean methods. Spring proxies it so calling a @Bean method twice still returns the same singleton.

Both read values from application.properties /.yml. @Value("${app.name}") – inject a single value. @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app") – bind a group of properties into a class (type-safe, better for many values).
Creates the bean only when it's first needed instead of at startup. Can also help break circular dependencies.

spring.q: What is a circular dependency? How to fix it?
spring.a: Bean A needs B and B needs A. Spring Boot 2.6+ fails by default. Fix: redesign (best — move the shared logic into a third class), use setter injection, or @Lazy on one dependency.

Aspect-Oriented Programming separates cross-cutting concerns (logging, security, transactions, performance timing) from business logic. You write the logic once and apply it to many methods. Terms: Aspect – the class with cross-cutting code (@Aspect). Advice – what to do and when: @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @Around. Pointcut – where to apply (expression like execution(* com.app.service.*.*(..))). Join point – a point in execution (method call). Weaving – linking aspects to code (Spring does it at runtime using proxies). @Aspect @Component public class LogAspect { @Around("execution(* com.shop.service.*.*(..))") public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint jp) throws Throwable { long s = System.currentTimeMillis(); Object r = jp.proceed(); System.out.println(jp.getSignature() + " took " + (System.currentTimeMillis()
- s) + "ms"); return r; } }

spring.q: JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB proxy?
spring.a: JDK proxy works only with interfaces. CGLIB creates a subclass of the class (works without interfaces). Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default. That's why final classes/methods can't be proxied.

spring.q: What is Spring MVC? Explain its flow.
spring.a:
A web framework based on Model-View-Controller.
1. Client sends request → DispatcherServlet (front controller).
2. DispatcherServlet asks HandlerMapping which controller handles the URL.
3. Controller method runs (calls service → repository).
4. Returns data (REST → converted to JSON by HttpMessageConverter/Jackson) or a view name.
5. For views, ViewResolver finds the page (JSP/Thymeleaf).
6. Response sent back to client.

spring.q: What is Spring Boot? Why use it?
spring.a:
Spring Boot is built on top of Spring and makes it fast and easy to create production-ready apps with almost no configuration. Key benefits: Auto-configuration – configures things automatically based on dependencies.
Starter dependencies – one dependency brings everything needed. Embedded server – Tomcat inside; run with java -jar app.jar, no WAR deploy. Actuator – health checks and metrics. Opinionated defaults, no XML.

Spring Spring Boot Lots of manual configuration (XML/Java config) Auto-configuration Need external server (deploy WAR) Embedded Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow Manage dependency versions yourself Starters manage compatible versions Slower to set up Quick start (start.spring.io)

It combines 3 annotations:
1. @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration) – the class can define beans.
2. @EnableAutoConfiguration – turns on auto-configuration.
3. @ComponentScan – scans the current package and sub-packages.

1. @EnableAutoConfiguration loads a list of auto-config classes from META- INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (older: spring.factories).
2. Each auto-config class has conditions, like:
3. @ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class) – only if this class is on the classpath.
4. @ConditionalOnMissingBean – only if you haven't defined your own bean.
5. @ConditionalOnProperty – only if a property is set.
6. So if you add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa + MySQL driver and DB URL, Boot automatically creates DataSource, EntityManagerFactory, TransactionManager.
7. Your own beans always win (because of @ConditionalOnMissingBean). Check what got configured with debug=true (condition evaluation report) or /actuator/conditions.

spring.q: How do you disable a specific auto-configuration?
spring.a: @SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) or spring.autoconfigure.exclude=... in properties.

Ready-made dependency bundles. Examples: spring-boot-starter-web – REST APIs, Spring MVC, embedded Tomcat, Jackson. spring-boot-starter-data-jpa – JPA + Hibernate. spring-boot-starter-security – Spring Security. spring-boot-starter-test – JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ. spring-boot-starter-actuator, -validation, -webflux, -thymeleaf.

spring.q: What happens when a Spring Boot app starts (SpringApplication.run)?
spring.a:
1. Creates a SpringApplication object and detects app type (servlet / reactive).
2. Prepares the Environment (reads properties, profiles).
3. Prints the banner.
4. Creates the ApplicationContext.
5. Loads bean definitions: component scanning + auto-configuration.
6. Refreshes the context – creates singleton beans, injects dependencies.
7. Starts the embedded web server (Tomcat on 8080).
8. Runs CommandLineRunner / ApplicationRunner beans.
9. App is ready (ApplicationReadyEvent).
Both run code right after startup (e.g., load sample data). CommandLineRunner gets raw String[] args; ApplicationRunner gets parsed ApplicationArguments.
Same purpose (configuration)..yml uses indentation/hierarchy and is more readable for nested config. If both exist,.properties takes priority.

spring.q: How do you change the default port?
spring.a: server.port=9090. Use server.port=0 for a random port.

Profiles let you have different config for different environments (dev, test, prod). Files: application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml. Activate: spring.profiles.active=prod or java -jar app.jar -- spring.profiles.active=prod. Beans for one profile: @Profile("dev").

spring.q: What is the order of property sources (priority)?
spring.a: Answer (high → low, simplified): Command-line args → OS environment variables → profile-specific properties outside jar → application.properties outside jar → profile- specific inside jar → application.properties inside jar → defaults. So you can override anything at deploy time without rebuilding.

spring.q: How can you change the embedded server?
spring.a:
Exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat from the web starter and add spring-boot-
starter-jetty or -undertow.
Developer tool for automatic restart when code changes, live reload, and dev-friendly defaults. Disabled automatically in production jars.

Adds production-ready endpoints to monitor and manage the app: /actuator/health – is the app up? (DB, disk) /actuator/info, /actuator/metrics, /actuator/env, /actuator/beans, /actuator/loggers, /actuator/mappings, /actuator/prometheus. Expose with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics. Secure them in production.

spring.q: What is a fat jar / how do you deploy a Spring Boot app?
spring.a: mvn clean package creates an executable jar with all dependencies and the embedded server inside. Run it with java -jar app.jar. Deploy on EC2, Docker/Kubernetes, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, ECS. You can also build a WAR for an external server by extending SpringBootServletInitializer.
start.spring.io – a website that generates a ready Spring Boot project with chosen dependencies, Java version, and build tool.
Both are build tools. Maven uses XML (pom.xml), fixed life cycle (clean, compile, test, package, install, deploy). Gradle uses Groovy/Kotlin DSL, faster incremental builds, more flexible.

spring.q: What is REST? What are its principles?
spring.a: REST (Representational State Transfer) is a style for building web APIs over HTTP. Principles: client-server, stateless (each request has all info), cacheable, uniform interface (resources identified by URLs), layered system.

Method Use Idempotent? GET Read data Yes POST Create new No PUT Replace/update whole resource Yes PATCH Partial update Not guaranteed DELETE Delete Yes Idempotent = calling it many times gives the same result as calling once.

200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not logged in), 403 Forbidden (logged in but no permission), 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 409 Conflict, 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable.
POST creates (new id each time). PUT replaces the whole object (send all fields). PATCH updates only the fields sent.

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/products") public class ProductController { private final ProductService service; public ProductController(ProductService service) { this.service = service; } @GetMapping public List<Product> all() { return service.findAll(); } @GetMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<Product> one(@PathVariable Long id) { return ResponseEntity.ok(service.findById(id)); } @PostMapping public ResponseEntity<Product> create(@Valid @RequestBody ProductDto dto) { return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(service.create(dto)); } @PutMapping("/{id}") public Product update(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody ProductDto dto) { return service.update(id, dto); } @DeleteMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable Long id) { service.delete(id); return ResponseEntity.noContent().build(); } }
@Controller returns a view name (HTML page). @RestController returns data (JSON/XML) directly because it adds @ResponseBody to every method.
@PathVariable reads from the URL path: /users/10 → id=10. @RequestParam reads query parameters: /users?page=2&size=10. Use path for identifying a resource, params for filtering/sorting/paging.
@RequestBody converts incoming JSON into a Java object. @ResponseBody converts the returned Java object into JSON. Jackson does the conversion.
Represents the full HTTP response – status code + headers + body. Gives you control: ResponseEntity.status(201).body(obj).

spring.q: How do you handle exceptions globally?
spring.a: Use @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods — one place to handle errors for all controllers and return clean error JSON. @RestControllerAdvice public class GlobalExceptionHandler { @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> notFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) { return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(Map.of("error", ex.getMessage())); } @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class) public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) { Map<String, String> errors = new HashMap<>(); ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(e -> errors.put(e.getField(), e.getDefaultMessage())); return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(errors); } } Spring 6 also supports standard ProblemDetail error responses (RFC 7807).

spring.q: How do you validate request data?
spring.a: Add spring-boot-starter-validation, put annotations on the DTO, and @Valid in the controller. public class UserDto { @NotBlank private String name; @Email private String email; @Min(18) private int age; @Size(min = 8) private String password; } Other annotations: @NotNull, @NotEmpty, @Pattern, @Past, @Positive. Custom validator: implement ConstraintValidator.

spring.q: Why use DTOs instead of returning entities directly?
spring.a: DTO (Data Transfer Object) controls exactly what goes in/out of the API. Benefits: hides sensitive fields (password), avoids lazy-loading/infinite recursion problems, decouples API from DB structure, allows validation. Map with MapStruct or ModelMapper.

spring.q: How do you implement pagination and sorting?
spring.a: @GetMapping public Page<Product> list(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page, @RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int size) { return repo.findAll(PageRequest.of(page, size, Sort.by("price").descending())); }

spring.q: How do you version a REST API?
spring.a: URL versioning /api/v1/users (most common), request param?version=1, header X-API-VERSION: 1, or media type (Accept: application/vnd.app.v1+json).

OpenAPI is a standard to describe REST APIs; Swagger UI shows interactive API docs where you can test endpoints. In Spring Boot add springdoc-openapi-starter- webmvc-ui → open /swagger-ui.html. (Your resume mentions RESTful APIs with OpenAPI documentation — be ready to show this.)

spring.q: How do you call another REST API from Spring Boot?
spring.a: RestTemplate (older, blocking), RestClient (Spring 6.1, modern blocking), WebClient (non-blocking, reactive), or OpenFeign (declarative interface – popular in microservices). @FeignClient(name = "inventory-service") public interface InventoryClient { @GetMapping("/api/inventory/{sku}") Inventory get(@PathVariable String sku); }

CORS allows a frontend on another domain (React on:3000) to call your API. Use @CrossOrigin(origins = "http://localhost:3000") on a controller or a global WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings() (and configure it in Spring Security if used).
Responses include links to related actions (e.g., "self", "orders"). Spring HATEOAS supports it. Rarely required but good to know.

Filter (Servlet level) runs before DispatcherServlet — used for security, logging, CORS. HandlerInterceptor (Spring MVC level) runs around controller methods — preHandle, postHandle, afterCompletion — used for auth checks, timing.

spring.q: What are JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA?
spring.a: JPA – a specification (set of rules/interfaces) for ORM in Java. Hibernate – the most popular implementation of JPA. Spring Data JPA – a layer on top that removes boilerplate: you write just an interface and get CRUD methods automatically. ORM = Object Relational Mapping (maps Java classes ↔ DB tables).

@Entity @Table(name = "products") public class Product { @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id; @Column(nullable = false, length = 100) private String name; private BigDecimal price; @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @JoinColumn(name = "category_id") private Category category; @Transient private String tempValue; // not saved in DB @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) private Status status; @CreationTimestamp private LocalDateTime createdAt; }

CrudRepository – basic CRUD (save, findById, findAll, deleteById, count). PagingAndSortingRepository – adds paging/sorting. JpaRepository – extends both + JPA extras (flush, saveAll, deleteAllInBatch, findAll(Sort)). Most projects use JpaRepository.

Spring creates the query from the method name: List<User> findByEmail(String email); List<User> findByAgeGreaterThanAndCity(int age, String city); List<Product> findTop5ByOrderByPriceDesc(); boolean existsByUsername(String u);

@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email =:email") // JPQL (uses entity names) User byEmail(@Param("email") String email); @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE city =?1", nativeQuery = true) // SQL (uses table names) List<User> byCity(String city); @Modifying @Transactional @Query("UPDATE User u SET u.active = false WHERE u.id =:id") int deactivate(@Param("id") Long id);
@OneToOne (User–Profile), @OneToMany / @ManyToOne (Customer–Orders), @ManyToMany (Student–Course, uses a join table). The side with @JoinColumn is the owning side; the other side uses mappedBy.

Lazy – related data is loaded only when you access it (better performance). Eager – loaded immediately with the parent. Defaults: @OneToMany /@ManyToMany = LAZY; @ManyToOne /@OneToOne = EAGER. Best practice: make everything LAZY and fetch what you need.
Happens when you access a lazy field after the session/transaction is closed (e.g., in the controller). Fix: fetch it inside the transaction, use JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph, or return DTOs.

spring.q: What is the N+1 query problem? How to fix it?
spring.a: You load 1 query for N customers, then Hibernate runs N more queries to load each customer's orders → 1 + N queries → slow. Fixes: JOIN FETCH in JPQL (SELECT c FROM Customer c JOIN FETCH c.orders), @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "orders"), @BatchSize, or DTO projections. Detect it by enabling spring.jpa.show-sql=true.

spring.q: What are entity states in Hibernate?
spring.a: Transient (new object, not in DB), Persistent/Managed (attached to the session; changes auto-saved), Detached (session closed), Removed (scheduled for delete).
Inside a transaction, Hibernate tracks managed entities. If you change a field, it automatically runs an UPDATE at commit — no need to call save().

spring.q: save() vs saveAndFlush()? persist() vs merge()?
spring.a: save() may delay the SQL until commit; saveAndFlush() sends it immediately. persist() makes a new entity managed; merge() copies a detached entity's state into a managed one and returns it.

spring.q: get() vs load() / findById() vs getReferenceById()?
spring.a: findById() hits the DB and returns Optional (empty if not found). getReferenceById() returns a lazy proxy without hitting the DB; throws EntityNotFoundException when accessed if the row is missing.

First-level – per session/transaction, on by default; same entity read twice → one query. Second-level – shared across sessions, off by default; enable with providers like Ehcache/Redis/Caffeine via JCache.
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto controls schema creation: none, validate, update, create, create-drop. Use validate /none in production and manage schema with Flyway or Liquibase.

Makes a method run in a database transaction — all operations succeed together or are all rolled back (ACID). Example: in a money transfer, debit and credit must both happen or neither. @Transactional public void transfer(Long from, Long to, BigDecimal amt) { accountRepo.debit(from, amt); accountRepo.credit(to, amt); // if this fails, debit is rolled back } Key points: By default it rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException/Error), not checked ones. Use @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class). It works via a proxy, so it doesn't work on self-invocation (calling a @Transactional method from the same class) and doesn't work on private methods. @Transactional(readOnly = true) for read methods = small performance boost.

Propagation Meaning REQUIRED (default) Join existing transaction, else create new REQUIRES_NEW Always start a new one (suspend the current) – e.g., audit log that must save even if main fails SUPPORTS Use a transaction if one exists, else run without MANDATORY Must have existing, else exception NOT_SUPPORTED Run without transaction (suspend current) NEVER Exception if a transaction exists NESTED Savepoint inside the current transaction

Control how transactions see each other's data: READ_UNCOMMITTED – can see uncommitted data (dirty reads). READ_COMMITTED – no dirty reads (default in PostgreSQL, Oracle). REPEATABLE_READ – same row gives same value within a transaction (default in MySQL). SERIALIZABLE – fully isolated, slowest. Problems they prevent: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read.

Optimistic – no lock; uses a @Version column; if someone else updated first, you get OptimisticLockException (good when conflicts are rare). Pessimistic – locks the row in DB (@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)), others wait (good for high-conflict data like seat booking).

spring.q: How do you connect Spring Boot to MySQL?
spring.a: spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/shopdb spring.datasource.username=root spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD} spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate spring.jpa.show-sql=true Boot uses HikariCP as the default connection pool.
A set of ready DB connections that are reused instead of opening a new one per request (opening is slow). Config: spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10.

spring.q: How do you optimize database queries in a Spring Boot app?
spring.a: (resume-related) Add indexes on columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY; avoid N+1 with fetch joins; use pagination; select only needed columns (DTO projections); use caching (@Cacheable + Redis); batch inserts (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size); check slow queries with EXPLAIN; use proper connection pool size. (On your resume: indexing + caching gave 30% and 25% improvements — explain which columns you indexed and what you cached.)

spring.q: How do you use MongoDB with Spring Boot?
spring.a: Add spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb, use @Document on the class, @Id, and extend MongoRepository<T, ID>. Set spring.data.mongodb.uri.
A framework for authentication (who are you?) and authorization (what are you allowed to do?). Protects against CSRF, session fixation, clickjacking, etc.

Authentication = verifying identity (login with username/password). Authorization = checking permissions (only ADMIN can delete). Authentication comes first. 401 = not authenticated; 403 = not authorized.

spring.q: How does Spring Security work internally?
spring.a:
1. Every request passes through a chain of Security Filters (SecurityFilterChain, via DelegatingFilterProxy / FilterChainProxy).
2. An authentication filter (e.g., UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter or your JWT filter) extracts credentials.
3. It calls the AuthenticationManager → AuthenticationProvider (e.g., DaoAuthenticationProvider).
4. The provider loads the user via UserDetailsService and checks the password with a PasswordEncoder (BCrypt).
5. On success, the Authentication object is stored in the SecurityContextHolder (ThreadLocal).
6. Authorization filter checks roles/permissions for the URL or method.

@Configuration @EnableWebSecurity @EnableMethodSecurity public class SecurityConfig { @Bean SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http, JwtFilter jwtFilter) throws Exception { http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()).sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)).authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.requestMatchers("/api/auth/**", "/swagger-ui/**").permitAll().requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN").anyRequest().authenticated()).addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class); return http.build(); } @Bean PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); } } (WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is removed in Spring Security 6.)

spring.q: What is JWT and how does JWT authentication work?
spring.a:
JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, signed token: header.payload.signature. Payload holds claims like user id, roles, expiry. Flow:
1. User logs in with username/password → server verifies.
2. Server creates a JWT signed with a secret key and returns it.
3. Client sends it in every request: Authorization: Bearer <token>.
4. A custom JWT filter (extends OncePerRequestFilter) validates the signature and expiry, loads the user, and sets the SecurityContext.
5. No session stored on the server → stateless, scales well in microservices. Use short-lived access tokens + refresh tokens. Don't put sensitive data in the payload (it's only Base64-encoded, not encrypted).

spring.q: How do you implement role-based access control (RBAC)?
spring.a: Assign roles to users (ROLE_USER, ROLE_ADMIN). Restrict by URL (hasRole("ADMIN")) or method: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')"), @PreAuthorize("#id == authentication.principal.id"). (Your BrewBean project has role-based auth — be ready to explain your roles and how you tested them.)

spring.q: What is CSRF? When can you disable it?
spring.a: Cross-Site Request Forgery — a malicious site tricks a logged-in browser into sending requests. Protection uses a CSRF token. You can disable it for stateless REST APIs using JWT (no cookies-based session), but keep it for session/cookie-based apps.
BCrypt is a slow, salted hash — each password gets a random salt, and the slowness makes brute-force attacks hard. Never store plain or MD5 passwords.

spring.q: What is OAuth2 and OpenID Connect?
spring.a: OAuth2 – authorization framework that lets an app access resources on behalf of a user without sharing the password ("Login with Google" gives an access token). OIDC – identity layer on top of OAuth2 (gives an ID token with user info). In Spring: spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client / oauth2-resource-server. Tools: Keycloak, Okta, AWS Cognito.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.q: What are microservices? Monolith vs Microservices?
spring.a: Microservices = building an app as small, independent services, each for one business function (user, order, payment), each with its own DB, deployed separately, communicating via REST or messaging. Monolith Microservices One big codebase & deployment Many small services Simple to start Complex (network, monitoring) Scale whole app Scale only the busy service One failure can crash all Failures isolated One tech stack Each service can use different tech

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.q: When should you NOT use microservices?
spring.a:
Small teams, simple apps, early-stage startups, or unclear domain boundaries. Microservices add network, deployment, and data-consistency complexity.
Start with a well-structured monolith and split later.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: A single entry point for all clients. It routes requests to the right service and handles cross-cutting stuff: authentication, rate limiting, logging, CORS, load balancing. Spring: Spring Cloud Gateway. AWS: API Gateway.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: Services register themselves (name + address) with a registry (Eureka Server). Other services find them by name instead of hard-coded IPs — important because instances come and go. Client: @EnableDiscoveryClient; on Kubernetes, K8s Services do this job.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: The calling service picks one instance from the registry list (round robin, etc.). Spring Cloud LoadBalancer does this (replaced Netflix Ribbon). Use @LoadBalanced on RestTemplate/WebClient or use Feign.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: A central config server that stores configuration for all services (in Git) so you can change config in one place without rebuilding services. Refresh with @RefreshScope / Spring Cloud Bus.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.q: What is the Circuit Breaker pattern?
spring.a: Prevents one failing service from bringing down others (cascading failure). Like an electrical circuit breaker: CLOSED – normal, requests go through. OPEN – too many failures → stop calling the service for some time, return a fallback immediately. HALF-OPEN – after a wait, allow a few test requests; if OK → CLOSED, else → OPEN again. Spring: Resilience4j. @CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory", fallbackMethod = "fallback") public Inventory check(String sku) { return inventoryClient.get(sku); } public Inventory fallback(String sku, Throwable t) { return Inventory.unknown(sku); } Related: Retry, Rate Limiter, Bulkhead, TimeLimiter.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: Synchronous – REST (Feign/WebClient/RestClient) or gRPC; caller waits for the response. Asynchronous – messaging with Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SQS/SNS; caller doesn't wait → loose coupling, better resilience.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.q: What is Kafka? How is it used with Spring Boot?
spring.a: Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform. Producers write messages to topics; consumers read them. Topics have partitions for scale; consumer groups share the load. kafkaTemplate.send("order-created", orderEvent); // producer @KafkaListener(topics = "order-created", groupId = "inventory") // consumer public void onOrder(OrderEvent e) {... }

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.q: How do you handle distributed transactions? Saga pattern?
spring.a: Each service has its own DB, so a normal @Transactional can't span services. The Saga pattern breaks it into local transactions with compensating actions if a step fails (e.g., payment fails → cancel order, release stock). Choreography – services react to each other's events (Kafka). Orchestration – a central orchestrator tells each service what to do. Two-phase commit (2PC) exists but is slow and rarely used in microservices.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: Each service owns its data so teams can change schemas independently and services stay loosely coupled. Other services get data via APIs or events, never by directly querying another service's DB.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: Tracks one request as it flows through many services using a trace ID and span IDs. Spring Boot 3 uses Micrometer Tracing (replaced Sleuth) with Zipkin/Jaeger/AWS X-Ray. Helps find which service is slow.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.q: How do you do centralized logging and monitoring?
spring.a: Logging: ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or AWS CloudWatch; include trace ID in logs. Monitoring: Actuator + Micrometer → Prometheus → Grafana dashboards, alerts.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.q: What is the difference between Docker and Kubernetes?
spring.a: Docker packages an app with everything it needs into a container (runs the same everywhere). Kubernetes manages many containers — deployment, scaling, self-healing, load balancing, rolling updates. spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: API Gateway, Service Registry, Circuit Breaker, Saga, CQRS (separate read and write models), Event Sourcing (store events, not just current state), Strangler Fig (migrate monolith piece by piece), Sidecar (helper container, e.g., service mesh like Istio), Outbox pattern (reliably publish events with DB changes).

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.a: Authenticate at the API Gateway (JWT/OAuth2), pass tokens to downstream services, use HTTPS/mTLS between services, keep secrets in a vault (AWS Secrets Manager), apply rate limiting, and least-privilege access.

spring.section: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud
spring.q: What is idempotency and why is it important in APIs?
spring.a: A request repeated many times has the same effect as once. Important for retries (e.g., a payment shouldn't be charged twice). Use an idempotency key header and store processed keys.

spring.q: How does caching work in Spring Boot?
spring.a: Enable with @EnableCaching, then: @Cacheable("products") – returns the cached result if present, else runs method and caches it. @CachePut – always runs and updates the cache. @CacheEvict – removes from cache (on update/delete). Providers: simple ConcurrentHashMap (default), Caffeine, Redis (distributed), Ehcache.
@EnableScheduling // on a config class @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *") // every day at 2 AM public void cleanup() {... } @Scheduled(fixedRate = 5000) // every 5 seconds

Runs a method in a background thread so the caller doesn't wait (e.g., sending email). Enable with @EnableAsync; return void or CompletableFuture. Like @Transactional, it doesn't work on self-invocation.

spring.q: What is Spring WebFlux? When to use it?
spring.a: Reactive, non-blocking web framework (Netty) using Mono (0–1 item) and Flux (0–N items). Good for high-concurrency, streaming, I/O-heavy apps. For normal CRUD apps, Spring MVC (or MVC + Java 21 virtual threads: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) is simpler.

Publish with ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(...)) and listen with @EventListener. @TransactionalEventListener runs only after the transaction commits. Good for decoupling inside one app.

spring.q: How do you test a Spring Boot application?
spring.a: Test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests. Unit test – JUnit 5 + Mockito, no Spring context, fast. Slice tests – @WebMvcTest (controllers only), @DataJpaTest (repositories with in- memory DB). Integration test – @SpringBootTest (loads full context) + Testcontainers (real MySQL in Docker).

spring.q: Write a unit test with Mockito.
spring.a: @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) class OrderServiceTest { @Mock OrderRepository repo; @InjectMocks OrderService service; @Test void shouldReturnOrderWhenFound() { when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(new Order(1L, "Coffee"))); Order o = service.getOrder(1L); assertEquals("Coffee", o.getItem()); verify(repo, times(1)).findById(1L); } @Test void shouldThrowWhenNotFound() { when(repo.findById(2L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty()); assertThrows(ResourceNotFoundException.class, () -> service.getOrder(2L)); } }
@Mock – pure Mockito mock (unit tests). @MockBean – replaces a bean inside the Spring context (Boot 3.4+ uses @MockitoBean). @Spy – real object where you can stub some methods.

spring.q: How do you test a controller with MockMvc?
spring.a: @WebMvcTest(ProductController.class) class ProductControllerTest { @Autowired MockMvc mvc; @MockitoBean ProductService service; @Test void getProduct() throws Exception { when(service.findById(1L)).thenReturn(new Product(1L, "Latte")); mvc.perform(get("/api/products/1")).andExpect(status().isOk()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("Latte")); } }

@Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll, @AfterAll, @DisplayName, @Disabled, @ParameterizedTest + @ValueSource /@CsvSource, @Nested, @Tag, @Timeout. Assertions: assertEquals, assertTrue, assertThrows, assertAll.

spring.q: What is code coverage? Which tool?
spring.a:
The percentage of code executed by tests. Tool: JaCoCo (with SonarQube for quality gates). High coverage is good, but meaningful tests (edge cases, failures) matter more than the number.

spring.q: Your API is slow. How do you find and fix the problem?
spring.a: 1) Measure – Actuator metrics, logs, APM/tracing to see which endpoint/step is slow. 2) Check DB – show-sql, slow query logs, EXPLAIN; fix N+1, add indexes, paginate. 3) Add caching for repeated reads. 4) Check external calls – add timeouts, async calls, circuit breakers. 5) Tune connection pool and thread pool. 6) Load test (JMeter/Gatling) to confirm the fix.

spring.q: How do you handle 1 million requests per day / scale a Spring Boot app?
spring.a: Keep services stateless (JWT, no sticky sessions), run multiple instances behind a load balancer with auto-scaling, cache hot data in Redis, use read replicas for DB, move slow work to queues (SQS/Kafka), use CDN for static content, and monitor.

Common reasons: exception is checked (use rollbackFor), exception is caught and swallowed inside the method, method is private or called from the same class (proxy bypassed), wrong transaction manager, or the DB table engine doesn't support transactions (MySQL MyISAM).

spring.q: How do you handle a service that's down in microservices?
spring.a: Timeouts + Retry (with backoff) + Circuit breaker + Fallback response; for async flows, put the message in a queue so it's processed when the service recovers; alert via monitoring.

spring.q: How do you secure sensitive configuration (passwords, keys)?
spring.a: Never commit them to Git. Use environment variables, AWS Secrets Manager / Parameter Store, HashiCorp Vault, or Kubernetes Secrets. Reference them in properties as ${DB_PASSWORD}.

spring.q: How do you prevent duplicate orders if a user clicks "Pay" twice?
spring.a: Disable the button on the UI, use an idempotency key on the API, a unique constraint in the DB, and optimistic locking.

spring.q: How would you design the BrewBean coffee e-commerce backend? (resume project) Answer (sample): Services: User/Auth (JWT + roles), Product catalog, Cart, Order, Payment, Notification. API Gateway in front, service discovery, each service with its own MySQL schema. Order → Payment via REST with circuit breaker, order events on Kafka for inventory and email. Product list cached in Redis. OpenAPI docs per service.
spring.a: Unit tests with JUnit/Mockito, integration tests with Testcontainers. Deployed on Docker/AWS.

spring.q: What is the difference between @RequestMapping and @GetMapping?
spring.a: @GetMapping is a shortcut for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET). Same for @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping.
Used when repositories/entities are outside the main application package. Normally Boot finds them automatically.

spring.q: How do you handle file uploads in Spring Boot?
spring.a: @PostMapping("/upload") public String upload(@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file) throws IOException { s3Client.putObject(b -> b.bucket("my-bucket").key(file.getOriginalFilename()), RequestBody.fromBytes(file.getBytes())); return "Uploaded"; } Limit size: spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=10MB.

spring.q: How do you log in Spring Boot?
spring.a: Default is SLF4J + Logback. private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class); (or Lombok @Slf4j). Set levels: logging.level.com.shop=DEBUG. Use structured/JSON logs in production with trace IDs.

A library that generates boilerplate at compile time: @Getter, @Setter, @Data, @NoArgsConstructor, @AllArgsConstructor, @RequiredArgsConstructor (great for constructor injection), @Builder, @Slf4j. Careful: @Data on JPA entities with relationships can cause infinite toString /hashCode loops.

spring.q: How do you avoid infinite recursion in JSON with bidirectional relationships?
spring.a: Use DTOs (best), or @JsonManagedReference / @JsonBackReference, or @JsonIgnore on one side.

spring.q: What is the difference between @Controller returning JSP (your BrewBean used JSP) and REST + React?
spring.a: JSP = server-side rendering; the server builds the HTML page. REST + React = server returns only JSON; the frontend builds the UI. REST separates frontend and backend, so mobile apps and other clients can reuse the same API.

aws.a: Using computing resources (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet, on demand, and paying only for what you use, instead of buying and maintaining your own hardware. Simple example: Like using electricity from the grid instead of running your own generator.

aws.q: What are the benefits of cloud computing?
aws.a: No upfront hardware cost (CapEx → OpEx), pay-as-you-go, scale up/down in minutes (elasticity), global reach in minutes, high availability, managed security, focus on business instead of servers.

aws.q: What are the cloud service models?
aws.a: Model You manage Provider manages AWS example IaaS OS, runtime, app, data Hardware, network, virtualization EC2, VPC, EBS PaaS App & data only Everything below Elastic Beanstalk, RDS SaaS Just use it Everything Amazon WorkMail, Chime FaaS / Serverless Just your function code Servers, scaling Lambda Pizza example: IaaS = buy ingredients and bake at home; PaaS = take-and-bake; SaaS = eat at the restaurant.

aws.q: What are the cloud deployment models?
aws.a: Public (AWS, Azure – shared infra), Private (only one organization), Hybrid (mix of on-premises + cloud, e.g., with AWS Outposts / Direct Connect), Multi-cloud (using multiple providers).
Amazon Web Services is the world's largest cloud platform, offering 200+ services — compute, storage, databases, networking, AI/ML, analytics, security — in data centers around the world.

aws.q: What are Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations?
aws.a: Region – a geographic area (e.g., ap-south-1 Mumbai, us-east-1 N. Virginia). Each is independent. Availability Zone (AZ) – one or more separate data centers inside a region with independent power/network. A region has usually 3+ AZs. Deploy across multiple AZs for high availability. Edge Location – small sites near users used by CloudFront (CDN) and Route 53 to deliver content faster. Also: Local Zones, Wavelength Zones for ultra-low latency.

aws.q: How do you choose a region?
aws.a: 1) Compliance / data laws (data must stay in the country), 2) Latency (close to users), 3) Service availability (not all services in all regions), 4) Price (varies by region).

aws.q: What is the AWS Shared Responsibility Model?
aws.a: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud — hardware, data centers, network, hypervisor. Customer is responsible for security IN the cloud — data, IAM users/permissions, OS patching on EC2, security groups, encryption settings, application code.

aws.q: What is the AWS Well-Architected Framework?
aws.a:
AWS's best-practice guide with 6 pillars:
1. Operational Excellence – automate, monitor, improve.
2. Security – protect data and systems.
3. Reliability – recover from failures, multi-AZ.
4. Performance Efficiency – use the right resources.
5. Cost Optimization – avoid waste.
6. Sustainability – reduce environmental impact.

aws.q: High availability vs Fault tolerance vs Scalability vs Elasticity?
aws.a: High availability – system stays up most of the time (multi-AZ). Fault tolerance – keeps working with zero interruption even if a part fails. Scalability – can handle growth (add resources). Elasticity – automatically adds/removes resources based on load.
Vertical (scale up) – bigger machine (t3.micro → m5.large); has a limit and needs downtime. Horizontal (scale out) – more machines behind a load balancer; preferred in the cloud.

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: You write code, and AWS runs it without you managing servers. Automatic scaling, pay only when code runs, built-in high availability. Servers still exist — you just don't see or manage them. Examples: Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, S3, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, Fargate.

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: A serverless compute service that runs your function in response to events and scales automatically. You pay per request and per GB-second of execution time. Languages: Java, Python, Node.js, Go,.NET, Ruby, or custom runtime/container image. Memory: 128 MB – 10 GB (CPU increases with memory). Max timeout: 15 minutes. Triggers: API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB Streams, SQS, SNS, EventBridge (cron), Kinesis, Cognito, etc. def lambda_handler(event, context): name = event.get("name", "World") return {"statusCode": 200, "body": f"Hello {name}"}

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.q: Explain your serverless facial emotion recognition project architecture.
aws.a:
1. User uploads an image → stored in an S3 bucket.
2. The S3 event triggers a Lambda function (Python).
3. Lambda preprocesses the image (OpenCV) and calls Amazon Rekognition DetectFaces with Attributes=['ALL'], which returns emotions (HAPPY, SAD, ANGRY, CALM, SURPRISED…) with confidence scores.
4. The result is saved (e.g., to DynamoDB/S3) and returned via API Gateway.
5. Logs and metrics go to CloudWatch.
6. IAM role gives Lambda least-privilege access to S3 and Rekognition. Why serverless: no servers to manage, auto-scales with uploads, pay only per image processed. Mention your results: 95.4% accuracy, ~300 ms latency at 10K requests/min, OpenCV preprocessing cut processing time by 40%. import boto3 rek = boto3.client("rekognition") def lambda_handler(event, context): rec = event["Records"][0]["s3"] resp = rek.detect_faces(Image={"S3Object": {"Bucket": rec["bucket"]["name"], "Name": rec["object"]["key"]}}, Attributes=["ALL"]) emotions = [max(f["Emotions"], key=lambda e: e["Confidence"]) for f in resp["FaceDetails"]] return {"statusCode": 200, "body": str(emotions)}

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.q: What is a Lambda cold start? How to reduce it?
aws.a: When Lambda hasn't run for a while (or scales up), AWS must create a new execution environment (download code, start runtime, run init code) → the first request is slower. Java has longer cold starts than Python. Reduce it: Provisioned Concurrency (keeps environments warm), Lambda SnapStart (for Java, Python,.NET – restores from a snapshot), smaller packages, fewer dependencies, initialise SDK clients outside the handler, more memory, lighter frameworks.

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: Number of requests handled at the same time. Default account limit ~1,000 per region (can be raised). Reserved concurrency – guarantees/limits concurrency for one function. Provisioned concurrency – pre-warmed environments. If the limit is exceeded → throttling (429).

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: A way to package shared libraries/dependencies separately (e.g., OpenCV, pandas) and reuse them across many functions. Up to 5 layers per function.

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: Sync (API Gateway, SDK RequestResponse) – caller waits for the result. Async (S3, SNS, EventBridge) – Lambda queues the event and retries on failure (2 retries), then sends failures to a DLQ or on-failure destination. Poll-based (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams) – Lambda polls the source via event source mapping.

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.q: How do you pass config/secrets to Lambda?
aws.a: Environment variables (encrypted with KMS), SSM Parameter Store, or Secrets Manager (use the Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension to cache).

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.q: When should you NOT use Lambda?
aws.a: Long jobs (>15 min), very steady high traffic (EC2/containers may be cheaper), need for GPUs, very low latency with no cold start tolerance, or apps needing persistent connections/state.

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: A fully managed service to create, publish, secure, and monitor APIs. It's the "front door" for Lambda or backend services. Features: throttling/rate limiting, API keys & usage plans, authorization (IAM, Cognito, Lambda authorizer), request validation, caching, CORS, stages (dev/prod), custom domains. Types: REST API (full features), HTTP API (cheaper, faster, simpler), WebSocket API (real-time chat).

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: Default integration timeout is 29 seconds (can now be increased for regional/private REST APIs). For long work, return quickly and process asynchronously (SQS + Lambda) — client polls or gets notified.

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: A serverless workflow orchestrator — connects Lambdas and other services into steps with branching, retries, parallel runs, and wait states, shown visually. Good for order processing, ML pipelines, Saga pattern. Types: Standard (long- running, up to 1 year) and Express (high volume, short).

aws.section: Serverless – Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions
aws.a: A serverless event bus that routes events from AWS services, your apps, or SaaS apps to targets based on rules. Also used for scheduled jobs (cron) via EventBridge Scheduler.

Simple Storage Service — object storage for any amount of data (images, videos, backups, logs, static websites). Data is stored as objects (file + metadata) in buckets. Bucket names are globally unique. Max object size 5 TB (use multipart upload for >100 MB). Durability: 99.999999999% (11 nines) – data is copied across multiple AZs. Unlimited storage, pay for what you store and transfer.

Class Use S3 Standard Frequently accessed data S3 Intelligent-Tiering Unknown/changing access – moves data automatically S3 Standard-IA Infrequent access, but fast when needed S3 One Zone-IA Infrequent, re-creatable data (single AZ, cheaper) S3 Express One Zone Ultra-fast, single-digit ms, single AZ S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval Archive, accessed ~once a quarter, ms retrieval S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Archive, minutes to hours retrieval S3 Glacier Deep Archive Cheapest, long-term (7–10 years), up to 12–48 hours retrieval
Rules to automatically move objects to cheaper classes or delete them after some days. Example: logs → Standard-IA after 30 days → Glacier after 90 days → delete after 1 year.

Keeps multiple versions of an object. Protects against accidental overwrite/delete (delete just adds a "delete marker"). Once enabled, it can only be suspended, not disabled. Combine with MFA Delete for extra safety.

aws.q: How do you secure an S3 bucket?
aws.a: Keep Block Public Access ON (default). Use IAM policies and bucket policies (least privilege). Encryption: SSE-S3 (default), SSE-KMS, SSE-C, or client-side; enforce HTTPS. Pre-signed URLs for temporary access. Enable versioning, access logs / CloudTrail, and Object Lock (WORM) if needed. ACLs are disabled by default (Object Ownership = bucket owner enforced).

A temporary URL that gives time-limited access to upload or download a private S3 object without making it public or sharing AWS credentials. Common for user uploads from the frontend directly to S3. url = boto3.client("s3").generate_presigned_url("get_object", Params={"Bucket": "my-bucket", "Key": "report.pdf"}, ExpiresIn=3600)
IAM policy is attached to a user/role ("what can this person do?"). Bucket policy is attached to the bucket ("who can access this bucket?") and can allow cross- account or public access.
Automatically copies objects to another bucket — CRR (Cross-Region) for disaster recovery/latency, SRR (Same-Region) for log aggregation or separate accounts. Versioning must be ON.

aws.q: How do you host a static website on S3?
aws.a: Upload HTML/CSS/JS, enable static website hosting, and (best practice) put CloudFront in front with Origin Access Control (OAC) so the bucket stays private, plus HTTPS via ACM.
Speeds up uploads from far-away users by routing through the nearest CloudFront edge location.
S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all PUTs and DELETEs (since Dec 2020) – after a successful write, a read immediately returns the latest data.

Elastic Block Store — a network hard disk (block storage) attached to an EC2 instance. Data persists after stopping the instance. Lives in one AZ. Types: gp3/gp2 (general SSD), io2/io1 (high IOPS SSD for DBs), st1 (throughput HDD), sc1 (cold HDD). Backups via snapshots (stored in S3, incremental, can be copied to other regions).
EBS – network storage, persistent. Instance store – physical disk on the host, very fast, but data is lost when the instance stops/terminates (good for cache/temp).

Elastic File System — a managed shared file system (NFS) that many EC2 instances (across AZs) and Lambda/containers can mount at the same time. Grows automatically. Linux only. (For Windows use FSx for Windows; for HPC use FSx for Lustre.)

S3 EBS EFS Object storage Block storage File storage Access via HTTP API Attached to one EC2 (mostly) Shared by many EC2 Unlimited, multi-AZ One AZ, fixed size Multi-AZ, auto-grows Images, backups, static sites OS disk, databases Shared content, CMS, home dirs Cheapest Medium Most expensive per GB

aws.q: What is AWS Storage Gateway / Snow family?
aws.a: Storage Gateway – connects on-premises storage with AWS (hybrid). Snowball/Snowcone – physical devices shipped to you to move huge data (TBs–PBs) into AWS when the network is too slow.

Relational Database Service — managed SQL databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, and Aurora. AWS handles setup, patching, backups, monitoring, and failover. You can't SSH into the DB server (except RDS Custom).

Multi-AZ Read Replica For high availability / disaster recovery For read performance / scaling Synchronous replication to standby in another AZ Asynchronous replication Standby is not used for reads (classic Multi-AZ instance) You can read from it Automatic failover (DNS switches) Manual promotion to become primary Same region Same or cross-region (up to 15 for Aurora, 15 for MySQL/PostgreSQL)

AWS's cloud-native relational DB, compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, up to ~5× faster than MySQL. Storage auto-grows up to 128 TB, 6 copies across 3 AZs, up to 15 read replicas, fast failover. Aurora Serverless v2 auto-scales capacity. Global Database for multi-region.
Automated backups – daily snapshot + transaction logs, point-in-time restore, retention 1–35 days. Manual snapshots – kept until you delete them. Restores always create a new DB instance.

A fully managed, serverless NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. Data in tables → items (rows) → attributes. Primary key: Partition key only, or Partition key + Sort key (composite). Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request) or Provisioned (RCU/WCU + auto scaling). Features: GSI/LSI (secondary indexes), DynamoDB Streams, TTL (auto-delete old items), DAX (in-memory cache, microseconds), Global Tables (multi-region, active- active), transactions, PITR backups.

aws.q: DynamoDB partition key design – why important?
aws.a: Data is spread across partitions by the partition key hash. Choose a key with many distinct values (userId, orderId) so load spreads evenly. A bad key (e.g., "status") creates hot partitions and throttling.

GSI (Global Secondary Index) – different partition key and sort key; can be created any time; own capacity; eventually consistent. LSI (Local Secondary Index)
– same partition key, different sort key; must be created with the table; supports strong consistency.
Query finds items by partition key (efficient, reads only matching items). Scan reads the whole table then filters (slow, expensive). Always design for Query.

aws.q: Strongly consistent vs eventually consistent reads?
aws.a: Eventually consistent (default, half the cost) – may return slightly old data for a moment. Strongly consistent – always the latest data (not supported on GSIs).

RDS DynamoDB Relational (SQL), fixed schema NoSQL, flexible schema Joins, complex queries, transactions Key-based access, very fast at scale Scales vertically + read replicas Scales horizontally automatically Banking, ERP, e-commerce orders Sessions, carts, IoT, gaming leaderboards, high traffic

Managed in-memory cache — Redis/Valkey (rich data types, persistence, replication, pub/sub) or Memcached (simple, multi-threaded). Used to cache DB results, sessions, leaderboards → reduces DB load and latency.

Redshift – data warehouse (analytics, OLAP). DocumentDB – MongoDB- compatible. Neptune – graph DB. Keyspaces – Cassandra-compatible. Timestream – time-series. MemoryDB – durable Redis. OpenSearch – search and log analytics. QLDB – ledger (being retired).

Database Migration Service — migrates databases to AWS with minimal downtime (e.g., on-prem MySQL → RDS). SCT (Schema Conversion Tool) converts schemas between different engines (Oracle → PostgreSQL).

Virtual Private Cloud — your own private, isolated network inside AWS where you launch resources. You control IP ranges (CIDR, e.g., 10.0.0.0/16), subnets, route tables, and gateways. Each region has a default VPC.

A public subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway (resources can have public IPs — e.g., load balancers, bastion host). A private subnet has no direct internet route (e.g., app servers, databases). Private instances reach the internet (for updates) via a NAT Gateway placed in a public subnet.

Internet Gateway (IGW) – allows two-way internet traffic for public subnets. NAT Gateway – allows private instances to go out to the internet, but blocks incoming connections from the internet. NAT Gateway is managed, AZ-specific (create one per AZ for HA); older option is a NAT instance.

aws.q: Design a typical 3-tier architecture in AWS.
aws.a: Users → Route 53 (DNS) → CloudFront (CDN + WAF) → Application Load Balancer (public subnets, 2+ AZs) → EC2 Auto Scaling Group / ECS running Spring Boot (private subnets) → RDS MySQL Multi-AZ + ElastiCache Redis (private DB subnets) Static files → S3. Secrets → Secrets Manager. Logs → CloudWatch. Security groups: ALB allows 443 from internet; App allows 8080 only from ALB SG; DB allows 3306 only from App SG.
Rules that decide where network traffic from a subnet goes. E.g., 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxx makes a subnet public; 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxx gives a private subnet outbound internet.
A small EC2 in a public subnet used as a secure "jump box" to SSH into private instances. Today, SSM Session Manager is preferred (no open ports, no keys, fully logged).

aws.q: What is VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway?
aws.a: VPC Peering – private connection between two VPCs (not transitive: A–B and B–C doesn't mean A–C). Transit Gateway – a central hub that connects many VPCs and on-prem networks (hub-and-spoke), simpler at scale.

Let private resources access AWS services without going through the internet. Gateway endpoints – S3 and DynamoDB (free). Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) – most other services (ENI with private IP, paid).

aws.q: How do you connect on-premises to AWS?
aws.a: Site-to-Site VPN (encrypted over the internet, quick to set up) or AWS Direct Connect (dedicated private fiber line — consistent speed, lower latency, more expensive). Client VPN for individual users.
Capture IP traffic info (source, destination, port, accept/reject) for a VPC/subnet/ENI into CloudWatch Logs or S3 — used for security analysis and troubleshooting connectivity.

AWS's managed DNS service (port 53) — converts domain names to IP addresses, registers domains, and does health checks. Routing policies: Simple, Weighted (e.g., 90/10 for canary), Latency-based (nearest region), Failover (active-passive DR), Geolocation, Geoproximity, Multivalue answer, IP-based. Records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME, Alias (AWS-specific; points to ELB/CloudFront/S3, works at the root domain, free queries), MX, TXT, NS.

AWS's CDN (Content Delivery Network) — caches content at edge locations worldwide so users get it faster. Origins: S3, ALB, EC2, any HTTP server. Features: HTTPS, WAF and Shield integration, signed URLs/cookies, Lambda@Edge / CloudFront Functions, OAC to keep S3 private.

Gives 2 static anycast IPs and routes users over AWS's private global network to the nearest healthy endpoint — improves performance for TCP/UDP apps (non-HTTP too). CloudFront caches content; Global Accelerator doesn't cache.

Identity and Access Management — controls who can access AWS (authentication) and what they can do (authorization). It's a global service and free. Users – a person or app with long-term credentials. Groups – collection of users (e.g., Developers) sharing permissions. Roles – temporary permissions assumed by AWS services (EC2, Lambda), other accounts, or federated users. No long-term keys. Policies – JSON documents defining permissions.

aws.q: What does an IAM policy look like?
aws.a: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*", "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "true"}} }] } Parts: Effect (Allow/Deny), Action, Resource, optional Condition, Principal (in resource policies).

aws.q: How is an IAM policy evaluated?
aws.a: 1) By default everything is denied (implicit deny). 2) An explicit Allow grants access. 3) An explicit Deny always wins over any allow. Also SCPs, permission boundaries, and session policies can limit permissions.

A user is a permanent identity with a password/access keys. A role is assumed temporarily and gives short-term credentials via STS. Always use roles for EC2, Lambda, ECS — never store access keys in code.

Don't use the root account for daily work (enable MFA, lock it away); least privilege; use roles instead of access keys; enable MFA; use groups; rotate credentials; use IAM Identity Center (SSO) for people; review with IAM Access Analyzer; audit with CloudTrail.
Security Token Service — issues temporary credentials (AssumeRole, GetSessionToken, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity). Used for roles, cross-account access, and federation.

Organizations manages many AWS accounts centrally with consolidated billing. Service Control Policies (SCPs) set maximum permissions for accounts (e.g., "no one can use regions outside India"). Control Tower sets up a secure multi-account landing zone.

Key Management Service — creates and manages encryption keys used by S3, EBS, RDS, Lambda, etc. Keys never leave KMS unencrypted. Uses envelope encryption (a data key encrypts data; the KMS key encrypts the data key). Supports key rotation and access control via key policies. CloudHSM = dedicated hardware for stricter compliance.

aws.q: Encryption at rest vs in transit?
aws.a: At rest – data stored on disk is encrypted (S3 SSE, EBS/RDS encryption with KMS). In transit – data moving over the network is encrypted (HTTPS/TLS, certificates from ACM – AWS Certificate Manager).

aws.q: Secrets Manager vs SSM Parameter Store?
aws.a: Secrets Manager Parameter Store Built for secrets (DB passwords, API keys) Config values + secrets (SecureString) Automatic rotation (e.g., RDS passwords) No built-in rotation Paid per secret Standard tier free Cross-region replication —

Adds sign-up / sign-in / user management to web and mobile apps. User Pools – user directory, login, JWT tokens (ID, access, refresh), MFA, social logins (Google, Facebook). Identity Pools – give users temporary AWS credentials to access AWS services directly (e.g., upload to S3).

aws.q: What are AWS WAF, Shield, GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie?
aws.a: WAF – web application firewall; blocks SQL injection, XSS, bad IPs, rate-based rules (on CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway). Shield – DDoS protection (Standard free for all; Advanced paid with 24/7 response team). GuardDuty – threat detection using ML on CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs. Inspector – scans EC2, containers, and Lambda for software vulnerabilities. Macie – finds sensitive data (PII) in S3. Security Hub – central dashboard of security findings. AWS Config – tracks resource configuration changes and checks compliance rules.

Simple Queue Service — a fully managed message queue to decouple services. A producer sends messages; consumers poll and process them. Standard queue – nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO queue – exactly-once processing, strict order, lower throughput (with batching/high-throughput mode more). Visibility timeout – after a consumer receives a message, it's hidden from others for a period (default 30s); if not deleted in time, it reappears. DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) – messages that fail too many times move here for investigation. Message retention: 1 min – 14 days (default 4 days). Max message size 256 KB (larger with S3 extended client). Long polling reduces empty responses and cost.
Simple Notification Service — pub/sub messaging. A publisher sends one message to a topic; SNS pushes it to all subscribers: SQS, Lambda, HTTP endpoints, email, SMS, mobile push.

aws.q: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Kinesis?
aws.a: SQS SNS EventBridge Kinesis Data Streams Queue (pull) Pub/sub (push) Event bus with rules (push) Real-time data stream One consumer group processes each message Fan-out to many subscribers Content-based routing, SaaS/AWS events, schedules Ordered records per shard, replay, many consumers Decouple & buffer work Notifications, fan- out Event-driven architectures Clickstreams, logs, IoT analytics Fan-out pattern: SNS topic → multiple SQS queues (e.g., order placed → inventory queue, email queue, analytics queue).

Real-time streaming data services: Data Streams (custom real-time processing, shards), Data Firehose (loads streaming data into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch with no code), Managed Service for Apache Flink (real-time SQL/Java analytics), Video Streams. For Kafka users there's Amazon MSK.
Managed ActiveMQ / RabbitMQ brokers — useful when migrating existing apps that use standard protocols (JMS, AMQP, MQTT) without rewriting to SQS/SNS.

ECS (Elastic Container Service) – AWS's own container orchestrator; simpler, deep AWS integration. EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) – managed Kubernetes; portable, huge ecosystem, more complex. Fargate – serverless compute for containers – runs ECS/EKS tasks without managing EC2 instances. ECR (Elastic Container Registry) – stores Docker images (like Docker Hub, private). App Runner – simplest way to run a container/web app from source or image.

aws.q: How would you deploy a Spring Boot application on AWS?
aws.a:
Answer (options):
1. EC2 – copy jar, run with systemd; put behind ALB + Auto Scaling.
2. Elastic Beanstalk – upload jar; everything managed.
3. ECS Fargate – build Docker image → push to ECR → ECS service behind ALB (common in companies).
4. EKS – for Kubernetes shops.
5. Lambda – with Spring Cloud Function / SnapStart for light APIs. CI/CD: GitHub push → CodePipeline/GitHub Actions → build & test (CodeBuild/Maven) → Docker image to ECR → deploy (ECS rolling / blue-green with CodeDeploy). DB on RDS, secrets in Secrets Manager, logs in CloudWatch.

aws.q: What are AWS CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CodePipeline?
aws.a: AWS's CI/CD tools. CodeBuild – builds and tests code (buildspec.yml). CodeDeploy – deploys to EC2, on-prem, Lambda, ECS (in-place, rolling, blue/green, canary). CodePipeline – connects all stages into an automated pipeline. CodeCommit – Git hosting (closed to new customers since 2024; most use GitHub/GitLab).

aws.q: Blue/green vs rolling vs canary deployment?
aws.a: Rolling – update instances a few at a time; no extra cost; mixed versions briefly. Blue/green – run the new version (green) alongside old (blue), switch traffic all at once; instant rollback. Canary – send a small % (e.g., 10%) to the new version first, then gradually increase if healthy.

aws.q: What is Infrastructure as Code? CloudFormation vs Terraform vs CDK?
aws.a: IaC = creating infrastructure using code/templates instead of clicking in the console → repeatable, version-controlled, reviewable. CloudFormation – AWS native, YAML/JSON templates → stacks; drift detection, change sets, rollback. CDK – write infrastructure in Java/Python/TypeScript; generates CloudFormation. SAM – simplified CloudFormation for serverless (Lambda, API Gateway). Terraform – by HashiCorp, multi-cloud, HCL language, state file.
A set of tools to manage EC2 and on-prem servers: Session Manager (shell access without SSH), Patch Manager, Run Command, Parameter Store, Automation, Inventory.

AWS's monitoring and observability service. Metrics – CPU, network, request count, custom metrics (e.g., orders per minute). EC2 memory/disk needs the CloudWatch Agent. Alarms – trigger actions when a metric crosses a threshold (send SNS email, scale ASG, stop instance). Logs – collect application and Lambda logs; search with Logs Insights; metric filters. Dashboards – visualize. Events – now EventBridge. Also: Synthetics (canaries), ServiceLens, Container Insights, Application Signals.

aws.q: CloudWatch vs CloudTrail vs AWS Config?
aws.a:
CloudWatch CloudTrail AWS Config Performance monitoring
– "How is it running?" Audit log of API calls – "Who did what, when, from where?" Configuration history & compliance – "What did it look like, is it compliant?" Metrics, logs, alarms e.g., "User X deleted bucket Y at 10:05 from IP Z" e.g., "Is encryption enabled on all EBS volumes?"

Distributed tracing — follows a request across API Gateway, Lambda, microservices, and databases, and shows a service map with latency and errors. Helps find bottlenecks. (Now also via OpenTelemetry / ADOT.)

aws.q: How do you optimize AWS costs?
aws.a: Right-size instances (Compute Optimizer), use Savings Plans/Reserved for steady load and Spot for flexible jobs, Auto Scaling + turn off dev resources at night, S3 lifecycle and Intelligent-Tiering, delete unused EBS volumes/snapshots/Elastic IPs, use serverless for spiky workloads, use Graviton (ARM) instances, reduce data transfer (CloudFront, VPC endpoints). Tools: Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets (alerts), Trusted Advisor, Cost and Usage Report, cost allocation tags.
Gives recommendations on cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits, and operational excellence. Full checks need Business/Enterprise support.
Lets new accounts try AWS services for free within limits (some always-free like Lambda 1M requests/month; newer accounts get credits-based free plans). Set a Budget alert to avoid surprise bills.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective) – how long the system can be down after a disaster. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) – how much data (in time) you can afford to lose. Example: RPO 1 hour = backups at least every hour.

Strategy Cost RTO/RPO Backup & Restore Lowest Hours Pilot Light (core DB running, rest off) Low Tens of minutes Warm Standby (smaller full copy running) Medium Minutes Multi-site Active/Active Highest Near zero

aws.q: What is decoupling and why is it important?
aws.a: Separating components so they don't depend directly on each other (using SQS, SNS, EventBridge). If one part is slow or down, others keep working and messages wait in the queue. Improves scalability and fault tolerance.

aws.q: What is a stateless application and why prefer it in AWS?
aws.a: The server doesn't store user session data locally; state lives in a DB/cache (DynamoDB, ElastiCache) or a token (JWT). Any instance can serve any request → easy auto scaling and load balancing.

aws.q: What are Amazon AI/ML services? (useful for AI roles)
aws.a: Rekognition (image/video analysis, faces, emotions, labels), Textract (extract text/forms from documents), Comprehend (NLP sentiment, entities), Polly (text-to-speech), Transcribe (speech-to-text), Translate, Lex (chatbots), SageMaker (build/train/deploy ML models), Amazon Bedrock (managed foundation/generative AI models via API, knowledge bases, agents), Amazon Q (AI assistant).

aws.q: Your EC2 website is not reachable. How do you troubleshoot?
aws.a: Check in order: instance is running and status checks pass → Security Group allows port 80/443 → NACL allows inbound and outbound ephemeral ports (1024–65535) → subnet's route table has a route to the Internet Gateway → instance has a public IP/Elastic IP → app/web server is actually running and listening (systemctl status, curl localhost) → OS firewall → DNS record correct. If behind ALB, check target group health checks.

aws.q: The app on EC2 in a private subnet can't download updates.
aws.a: Why? A private subnet has no Internet Gateway route. Add a NAT Gateway in a public subnet and a route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT in the private route table (or use VPC endpoints for AWS services like S3).

aws.q: How do you give an EC2 application access to S3 securely?
aws.a: Create an IAM role with a least-privilege S3 policy, attach it to the EC2 via an instance profile. The SDK picks up temporary credentials automatically. Never hard-code access keys.

aws.q: Your Lambda is timing out. What do you check?
aws.a: Increase timeout (max 15 min) and memory (more CPU), check slow downstream calls (DB, API) and add timeouts, reuse connections by creating clients outside the handler, check if Lambda in a VPC can reach the internet/services (needs NAT or VPC endpoints), look at CloudWatch Logs and X-Ray. For long jobs → Step Functions, SQS batching, or ECS/Fargate.

aws.q: How do you design a scalable image upload + processing system? (like your project)
aws.a: Frontend gets a pre-signed URL → uploads directly to S3 → S3 event → SQS (buffer) → Lambda processes (resize, Rekognition) → metadata into DynamoDB → notify user via SNS/WebSocket. Serve images through CloudFront. Failures go to a DLQ. Everything scales automatically, pay per use.

aws.q: Traffic suddenly spikes 10× during a sale. How does your architecture handle it?
aws.a: CloudFront caches static content; ALB + Auto Scaling (maybe scheduled/predictive scaling before the sale); ElastiCache for hot reads; RDS read replicas / Aurora; SQS to queue orders so the DB isn't overloaded; DynamoDB on- demand for carts; WAF rate limiting against bots; load test in advance.

aws.q: How do you make an application highly available across AZs?
aws.a: Run instances in at least 2 AZs via an ASG, use an ALB across those AZs, RDS Multi-AZ, S3/DynamoDB (multi-AZ by default), NAT Gateway per AZ, and health checks everywhere. For region-level failure: cross-region replicas + Route 53 failover.

aws.q: Someone accidentally deleted important S3 files. How do you prevent it next time?
aws.a: Enable versioning (restore previous versions), MFA Delete, Object Lock, least-privilege IAM (no s3:DeleteObject for most users), cross-region replication backup, and CloudTrail data events to see who deleted.

aws.q: Your AWS bill suddenly went up. What do you do?
aws.a: Open Cost Explorer grouped by service/region/tag to find the cause, check for forgotten resources (large EC2, NAT Gateway data, unattached EBS, idle RDS, data transfer), set AWS Budgets alerts and Cost Anomaly Detection, then right-size or delete.

aws.q: How do you store and rotate DB credentials for a Spring Boot app on AWS?
aws.a: Store in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation for RDS; give the app's IAM role permission to read that secret; use Spring Cloud AWS to load it into spring.datasource.*. Or use RDS IAM authentication (no passwords).

aws.q: What would you do if an access key was leaked on GitHub?
aws.a: Immediately deactivate/delete the key, check CloudTrail for what it was used for, remove any resources created by attackers, rotate other credentials, and move to IAM roles + a secrets scanner (git-secrets) to prevent it again. AWS also detects and notifies about exposed keys.

aws.q: Monolith to microservices migration on AWS – how?
aws.a: Use the Strangler Fig pattern: put an ALB/API Gateway in front, extract one module at a time (e.g., payments) into its own service on ECS/Lambda with its own DB, route its URLs to the new service, keep the rest in the monolith, and repeat. Use SQS/SNS/EventBridge for async communication.
